Losing weight and acquiring self-control is fucking complicated. Lots of people here like to reduce it to a moral issue, as if good people are fit and worthless people are fat. This is horribly reductive and oversimplifying, and if you buy into it, OP, you're not going to succeed. You'll get discouraged, and instead of seeing weight loss as a skill you must develop--through fucking it up a lot at first but sticking with it until you get the hang of it--if you on the contrary view it as binary matter of identity, either worthy or worthless, you'll assume you're worthless after your first inevitable setback.

Rather, adopt as your identity somebody who is learning to lose weight, somebody who is in the process of imperfectly but persistently habituating yourself to a more and more healthy lifestyle.

A large part of this that is severely overlooked is psychological in nature. The set of habits that got you fat did not just drop out of the fucking sky. A lot of the American relationship with food is as a coping mechanism for stress. The Adverse Childhood Experiences Study is a decent place to start in terms of evaluating what sort of bullshit in the back of your brain may be fucking you up and hitting you with cortisol at times when you wouldn't expect it, like stress-eating on Mother's Day because you no longer talk to your mother since she's a cunt, for example.

Then you can evaluate your present life and see what kind of stressors are currently operating there: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holmes_and_Rahe_stress_scale

Once you have an idea of how the deck has been stacked against you, you can maybe take it easy on yourself in terms of your identity. You could at this point seize on these as excuses, but I have about 7 ACEs and just spent the last few years clocking in 400-500+ LCUs annually, and I just lost ten pounds, bitches. The bottom line is that your weight is probably not your fault, but it nevertheless is your problem. Many things in life are like this. It's not fair, but you're the one who'll suffer unless you change it. The point is that you can change it. You've probably had lots of setbacks and countervailing circumstances. You need an actual plan, not just a determination, because your free will is a finite resource. Unless you have an intelligent plan that you can actually execute, when you get hungry enough and stressed out enough, you will run out of willpower, you'll eat a bunch of shit, and in the aftermath, you'll feel as if you are, in your essence, a failure. Losing weight is especially rough from a Decision Fatigue angle because studies have shown a spike in willpower after lunch, indicating that it's easier to make decisions when your blood sugar is high.

Toward that end, you have to make decisions ahead of time, such as making sure you don't have ANY junk food left in the house beforehand. You also need to have healthy food you can snack on when you get cravings, full of lean protein and fiber.

You are big enough you can fuck up your joints and shit if you're not careful. Do not just start off sprinting HIITs because they're awesome. They ARE awesome, but you have to work up to them.

TALK TO YOUR DOCTOR.

Discuss what an appropriate ramp-up trajectory for you looks like. Seriously, the impacts on your feet, ankles, and knees from carrying excess weight are exponential multipliers of your extra weight. The last thing you want to do is hurt yourself trying to run too soon such that you can never really run again.

I recommend looking into swimming or rowing for your initial cardio stuff. A Concept 2 rowing machine can be found on Craigslist--usually they hold their value very well (which is why you're buying one) but occasionally you can find a real deal at an estate sale or whatever. Failing that, usually there's a pool at the Y. Go swim. It's fucking boring, but you can do HIIT sprints and won't kill your joints. If you need to look up HIIT stuff, check out Tabata circuits. As for resistance, it really would be best if you could get a Y membership or something on the cheap. Whatever you do, try not to have any zero days. Even if all you do is one pushup, or one 15 minute yoga sequence, you'll keep the ball rolling, and get back on the wagon tomorrow. You WILL need rest and recovery days.
